questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Area marked in the given image is supplied by dermatome number?
questions.explanation:
The marked dermatome which includes the umbilicus is supplied by T10.

The dermatomal distribution of the abdominal region is: T7-T9 supply skin from the xiphoid process to just above the umbilicus; T10 supplies skin around the umbilicus; T11-T12 supply skin below the umbilicus up to the suprapubic region; L1 supplies skin around the genitalia and upper medial thigh.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: During the abdominal examination of a patient, you notice the following pattern of subcutaneous venous circulation. In which of the following conditions is this pattern seen?
questions.explanation:
The pattern of subcutaneous venous circulation depicted in the image can be seen in cases of inferior vena caval obstruction.

The level of the umbilicus is a watershed area for venous and lymphatic circulation. The systemic veins anastomose with tributaries of portal veins at the umbilicus. Normally, venous blood and lymphatics flow upwards above the plane of the umbilicus and downwards below this plane.

The source figure contrasts portal hypertension (radiating away from the umbilicus like a star/caput medusae), inferior vena caval obstruction, superior vena caval obstruction, and portal obstruction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 25-year-old woman having lower abdominal pain and shock is diagnosed with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy. The gynecologist decides to perform an emergency laparotomy via the incision shown in the image below. Which of these structures is not incised in this approach?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a midline incision used for emergency laparotomy. Transversus abdominis muscle is not incised in this approach.

Layers pierced in the midline approach, superficial to deep: skin; superficial fascia (Camper's and Scarpa); linea alba; transversalis fascia; extraperitoneal fat; parietal peritoneum. There are no muscles pierced in this approach.

Layers pierced in a flank approach, superficial to deep: skin; superficial fascia (Camper's and Scarpa); external oblique; internal oblique; transversus abdominis; transversalis fascia; extraperitoneal fat; parietal peritoneum.

Clinical note: umbilical and epigastric hernia can occur due to a congenital or acquired defect in the linea alba such as a midline abdominal incision.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A 70-year-old man complains of weakness of his trunk muscles following a stroke. While examining the patient, you ask him to perform the following movement. Which of the following muscles is/are being tested here?

options.text: Ipsilateral external oblique and contralateral internal oblique
Ipsilateral external oblique and internal oblique
Ipsilateral transversus abdominis and internal oblique

questions.correctAnswerText: Ipsilateral external oblique and internal oblique
questions.explanation:
The given image shows lateral flexion of the trunk being performed, which is done by the ipsilateral external oblique (EO) and internal oblique (IO) muscles.

The anterior abdominal wall comprises four muscles: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, and rectus abdominis.

Movements: forward flexion of the trunk (lumbar spine) — rectus abdominis and bilateral IO and EO; lateral flexion — ipsilateral IO and EO; rotation — ipsilateral IO and contralateral EO; pulling the testes towards the superficial inguinal ring — cremaster.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: An anterior abdominal wall nerve block is to be performed for a patient with pain at the appendicectomy incision site. What is the site of injection of the local anesthetic?
questions.explanation:
The local anesthetic is injected between the internal oblique (marked 2) and transversus abdominis (marked 3) muscles in the anterior abdominal wall because the neurovascular plane lies between these muscles.

The plane contains the lower six thoracic nerves, iliohypogastric nerve, posterior intercostal and subcostal vessels, and anastomosis between superior and inferior epigastric arteries.

The transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is a regional anesthetic technique used for abdominal surgeries such as open cholecystectomy, open appendicectomy, and hernia surgery, and for postoperative analgesia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The given image of the rectus sheath represents a section at which of the following levels?

options.text: Below a point midway between pubic symphysis and umbilicus
Between the umbilicus and arcuate line
Below a point midway between xiphisternum and pubic symphysis

questions.correctAnswerText: Below a point midway between pubic symphysis and umbilicus
questions.explanation:
The image represents a transverse section through the rectus sheath below the arcuate line. The arcuate line is located midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis.

The rectus sheath is formed from the aponeuroses of external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis. Each aponeurosis is bilaminar.

Above the arcuate line: the anterior layer is formed by both leaves of external oblique and the anterior leaf of internal oblique; the posterior layer is formed by the posterior leaf of internal oblique and both leaves of transversus abdominis.

Below the arcuate line: the anterior layer is formed by aponeuroses of all three muscles; the posterior layer is deficient and rectus abdominis lies directly on transversalis fascia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: In the rectus sheath, with which of the following arteries does the superior epigastric artery anastomose?

options.text: Branch of superficial circumflex iliac artery

questions.explanation:
In the rectus sheath, the superior epigastric artery anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery.

The superior epigastric artery is a branch of the internal thoracic artery. They anastomose in the rectus sheath above the level of the umbilicus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: What is the nerve supply for the structure marked X in the below image?
questions.explanation:
The structure marked in the image is pyramidalis, supplied by the subcostal nerve (ventral ramus of T12).

Pyramidalis is a triangular muscle within the rectus sheath. Its base is attached to the anterosuperior margin of the pubis and ligamentous fibres in front of the symphysis, and its apex is attached to the linea alba.

It receives terminal branches of the subcostal nerve (T12). In some cases it may be innervated wholly or partly by fibres from L1 travelling in the subcostal or ilioinguinal nerves.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the boundaries of the inguinal canal is false?

options.text: Anterior wall has external oblique aponeurosis along its entire length
Posterior wall has transversalis fascia along its entire length
Roof has the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscle
External oblique is present in the anterior wall, roof, and posterior wall

questions.correctAnswerText: External oblique is present in the anterior wall, roof, and posterior wall
questions.explanation:
External oblique is present only in the anterior wall of the inguinal canal.

Internal oblique is present in the anterior wall in the lateral one-third (muscular fibres), roof (arched fibres), and posterior wall (as part of the conjoint tendon). Transversus abdominis is present as part of the roof and posterior wall (as the conjoint tendon).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the contents of the inguinal canal is true?

options.text: Internal spermatic fascia is derived from the fascia transversalis
Ilioinguinal nerve enters the canal at the deep inguinal ring
Cremasteric artery is a branch of superior epigastric artery
Indirect inguinal hernias do not occur in women

questions.correctAnswerText: Internal spermatic fascia is derived from the fascia transversalis
questions.explanation:
Internal spermatic fascia is a derivative of transversalis fascia. External spermatic fascia is derived from external oblique aponeurosis, and cremasteric fascia from internal oblique.

The ilioinguinal nerve does not enter the inguinal canal at the deep ring; it enters by piercing the posterior wall. The cremasteric artery is a branch of the inferior epigastric artery. Indirect inguinal hernias occur in both men and women.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: A man was brought to the emergency department after he fell into a manhole and injured his perineum. He was unable to pass urine and blood was seen at the tip of the urethra. A diagnosis of bulbar urethral injury was made. Where do you least expect the urine to get collected in this case?
questions.explanation:
In bulbar urethral injury, the medial portion of the thigh is the least likely site for collection of urine.

Rupture of the urethra below the urogenital diaphragm causes extravasation into the superficial perineal pouch, penis and scrotum in males or labia majora in females, and the anterior abdominal wall.

Below the umbilicus, superficial fascia divides into Camper's fatty layer and Scarpa's membranous layer. Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the membranous superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia). Colles' fascia attaches to fascia lata along Holden's line, extending laterally from the pubic tubercle; extravasated fluid cannot pass into the medial thigh below this line because of this firm attachment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.question: The image below shows the insertion of the transversus abdominis muscle. Identify the conjoint tendon.
questions.explanation:
The structure marked 3 is the conjoint tendon. It is formed from the lower fibres of internal oblique and the lower part of the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. It attaches to the pubic crest and extends variably along the pectineal line.

Transversus abdominis origin: internal surface of 7th-12th costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and connective tissue deep to the lateral third of the inguinal ligament. Insertion: linea alba with the aponeurosis of internal oblique, pubic crest, and pecten pubis via the conjoint tendon.
